# Abstract

Prehistoric Southeast Asia spans 4,12M km² (encompassing 4.116.175 km² across 52.603 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells), extending across mainland river basins, drowned continental shelves and insular volcanic archipelagos. Between 10000BC and 500BC, the region experienced profound environmental and social transformations: the post-glacial marine transgression that submerged Sundaland, the dispersal of Austroasiatic and Austronesian language families, the adoption of sedentary wet-rice agriculture and arboriculture, and the emergence of specialised bronze and iron metallurgical networks. These developments reshaped settlement systems from dispersed limestone rockshelters to permanent fortified farming communities and maritime coastal emporia.

Reconstructed across eight physiographic sub-regions under MANDALA, aggregate population grew from 420k terminal Pleistocene foragers in 10000BC to 580k in 8000BC and 950k in 6000BC, reflecting persistent Hoabinhian foraging and maritime littoral exploitation. Population expansion accelerated during the mid-Holocene Neolithic transition, climbing to 1,75M in 4000BC and 2,85M in 3000BC as agriculturalist migrations entered northern Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines. Growth intensified further during the Bronze and Iron Ages, reaching 4,2M in 2000BC, 6,4M in 1000BC and an all-time prehistoric apex of 8,5M inhabitants at 500BC (yielding an aggregate density of 206,5 persons per 100 km²).

Demographic mass coalesced along nutrient-rich alluvial plains and volcanic islands. By 500BC, the Red River Delta and Lower Mekong accommodated 1,53M people (18% of regional population; 305,93 persons per 100 km²), anchored by the Dong Son and Sa Huynh cultural complexes. The volcanic terraces of Java, Bali and the Sunda Arc supported 1,45M inhabitants (17%; achieving the highest sub-regional density at 686,99 persons per 100 km²). The Chao Phraya basin, Khorat Plateau and Middle Mekong housed 1,19M people (14%; 157,12 persons per 100 km²), centred on major bronze-producing centres such as Ban Non Wat and Ban Chiang. The western river systems of the Irrawaddy and Salween supported 1,11M people (13%; 157,68 persons per 100 km²), while the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra accommodated 1,11M inhabitants (13%; 180,13 persons per 100 km²). The maritime insular provinces of the Philippines (935k; 310,74 persons per 100 km²), Wallacea and Timor (680k; 237,35 persons per 100 km²) and Borneo (510k; 68,29 persons per 100 km²) sustained lower aggregate densities, reflecting reliance on maritime foraging, swidden tuber cultivation and sago extraction.

This historical demographic synthesis integrates 523 catalogued archaeological settlements with ancient genomics, cranio-morphometrics, sediment pollen profiles and radiocarbon datasets. By subtracting nucleated settlement populations from environmental suitability rasters, the reconstruction reconciles local archaeological habitation sites with dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, establishing an empirical baseline for early Southeast Asian prehistory prior to classical state formation.

# Background

## Ecological Gradients and Post-Glacial Drowning of Sundaland

The prehistoric environment of Southeast Asia was defined by dramatic late Quaternary palaeogeographic alterations [@Piper2017Perspectiv; @Maxwell1999Holocene]. During the Last Glacial Maximum, sea levels were approximately 120 metres lower than present, exposing the vast continental shelf of Sundaland as a continuous landmass connecting Indochina, the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java and Borneo [@Curnoe2016Deep; @Piper2017Perspectiv]. Major river networks, including the North Sunda and East Sunda palaeorivers, drained expansive interior alluvial lowlands into the South China Sea and Java Sea.

Between 14000BC and 6000BC, rapid deglaciation and melting ice sheets drove rapid marine transgression, drowning over two million square kilometres of low-lying shelf [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Kaharudin2020Review]. This submergence fractured Sundaland into an archipelago of islands and peninsulas, shortening overland communication routes and expanding shallow coastal shelves, mangrove estuaries and coral reef ecosystems.

East of the Huxley-Wallace Line, deep oceanic trenches insulated the Wallacean islands (Sulawesi, the Moluccas, Flores and Timor) and the Philippines from continental land bridges throughout the Pleistocene, requiring maritime watercraft for human colonisation [@Carro2022Talking; @Carro2024Prehistori].

Mainland Southeast Asia retained large river systems: the Irrawaddy, Salween, Chao Phraya, Mekong and Red River. These rivers carried nutrient-rich silt from the Tibetan Plateau and Yunnan highlands, forming extensive floodplains subject to seasonal monsoon inundation [@Maxwell1999Holocene; @Pryce2025Southeast]. Interior plateaus, such as the Khorat Plateau of northeast Thailand and the Shan Plateau of eastern Myanmar, provided dry dipterocarp forest environments rich in wild game, salt domes and mineral ores [@Pryce2024Late; @Pryce2025Southeast].

## The Hoabinhian Technocomplex and Pre-Neolithic Foraging

During the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene (10000BC to 6000BC), hunter-gatherer populations across mainland and western insular Southeast Asia manufactured pebble-tool assemblages termed the Hoabinhian technocomplex [@Matsumura2008Terminal; @Piper2017Perspectiv]. Characterised by unifacially worked river cobbles (*sumatraliths*), split pebbles, bone points and shell scraping tools, Hoabinhian toolkits reflect broad-spectrum rainforest foraging [@Stimpson2025Year]. Populations exploited wild pigs, cervids, primates, freshwater molluscs and diverse tropical plants, including tubers (*Dioscorea*), legumes and wild fruits [@Matsumura2008Terminal; @Stimpson2025Year].

Habitation was concentrated in limestone karst rockshelters and cave systems, such as Hang Cho and Lang Bon in northern Vietnam, Spirit Cave and Tham Lod in northwestern Thailand, Gua Cha in peninsular Malaysia and Niah Cave in Sarawak [@Curnoe2016Deep; @Matsumura2008Terminal; @Aghakhanian2022Sequence]. Mortuary practices in these caves reveal flexed burials sprinkled with red ochre and accompanied by personal ornaments of perforated animal teeth and marine shells [@Carro2024Prehistori; @Hung2025Earliest].

At Tron Bon Lei on Alor Island in Wallacea, terminal Pleistocene circular burials document maritime foraging adaptations utilising fishhooks and marine shell ornaments [@Carro2022Talking].

Skeletal and cranio-morphometric analyses demonstrate that these early Holocene foragers exhibited robust cranial vaults, broad nasal apertures and alveolar prognathism allied to Australo-Papuan lineages [@Matsumura2008Terminal; @Matsumura2019Craniometr; @Matsumura2021Female]. Genetic studies confirm that contemporary indigenous populations, including the Semang of peninsular Malaysia and the Agta of the Philippines, carry deep ancestries descending from these basal Hoabinhian and pre-Neolithic foragers [@Aghakhanian2022Sequence; @Stoneking2023Genomic].

## Ceramic Typologies and Cultural Horizons

Ceramic technologies developed across multiple distinct chronological horizons in Southeast Asia [@Piper2017Perspectiv; @Nelson2020Tracing]:
- Early cord-marked and basket-impressed wares: Initial coarse earthenware emerged in hunter-gatherer contexts during the early to middle Holocene, notably in the Da But and Bac Son cultures of northern Vietnam and Spirit Cave in Thailand [@Matsumura2017Holocene; @Piper2017Perspectiv]. These thick-walled vessels served for boiling tubers, stews and shellfish.
- Phung Nguyen and related fine incised wares: From 2000BC, sophisticated incised, stamped and punctate ceramic traditions appeared in the Red River Delta and central Thailand, exhibiting geometric meanders, zone decoration and burnished surfaces [@Pryce2025Southeast].
- Painted wares of the Ban Chiang tradition: In the Khorat Plateau, distinctive red-painted geometric vessels appeared during the first millennium BC, accompanying bronze mortuary assemblages [@Pryce2025Southeast].
- Red-slipped Austronesian pottery: Expanding southward through the Philippines, Taiwan-derived red-slipped pottery with circle-stamped and dentate decorations spread into Sulawesi, the Moluccas and the Lesser Sunda Islands [@Wu2021Prehistori; @Suryatman2018Sakkarra].
- Sa Huynh jar-burial ceramics: Along the coastal littoral of central Vietnam, large ceramic burial jars accompanied by carinated bowls, pedestalled vessels and lids were deployed in extensive coastal cemeteries [@Wu2021Prehistori; @Carro2024Prehistori].

## Subsistence Packages and Botanical Domestication

The transition to sedentary life involved diverse subsistence strategies tailored to micro-ecological zones [@Fuller2011Pathways; @Piper2017Perspectiv; @Pryce2025Southeast]:
- Grain agriculture: In mainland river valleys, domesticated rice (*Oryza sativa*) and foxtail millet (*Setaria italica*) formed the energetic core of the Neolithic economy from 2500BC onward [@Wang2026Multiple; @Pryce2025Southeast]. Inundated fields and natural river backswamps supported seasonal harvesting.
- Vegeculture and arboriculture: Across insular Southeast Asia, grain cultivation was supplemented or replaced by root crops, including taro (*Colocasia esculenta*) and yams (*Dioscorea alata*), alongside tree crops such as coconut (*Cocos nucifera*), breadfruit (*Artocarpus*), banana (*Musa*) and sago palm (*Metroxylon sagu*) [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Piper2017Perspectiv].
- Animal husbandry: Domesticated pigs (*Sus scrofa*) and dogs accompanied Neolithic dispersals from southern China [@Stoneking2023Genomic]. Later, domestic water buffalo (*Bubalus bubalis*) and zebu cattle were incorporated to provide traction in wet-rice paddies and meat for ceremonial feasting.
- Marine exploitation: Coastal and island populations maintained intensive fishing of pelagic and reef taxa (tuna, jacks, parrotfish) using shell fishhooks, composite harpoons and woven nets [@Carro2022Talking; @Wu2021Prehistori].

## Mortuary Traditions and Social Differentiation

Mortuary practices across prehistoric Southeast Asia provide valuable bioarchaeological evidence for social organisation and demographic structure [@Carro2024Prehistori]:
- Flexed and crouched burials: Typical of early Holocene forager horizons at Hang Cho, Spirit Cave, Niah and Tron Bon Lei, individuals were placed in simple pits, often dusted with red haematite powder and accompanied by shell tools or game animal bones [@Matsumura2008Terminal; @Carro2022Talking].
- Extended supine burials with ceramic grave goods: From the third millennium BC, Neolithic cemeteries such as Man Bac, Ban Non Wat and Ban Chiang document extended supine burials arranged in family rows or corporate cemetery plots [@McColl2018Prehistori; @Pryce2025Southeast]. Skeletons were accompanied by ceramic vessels, polished stone adzes, shell beads and bone hairpins.
- Jar-burial traditions: Beginning around 1500BC and expanding rapidly by 800BC, secondary mortuary processing in earthenware jars emerged across coastal Vietnam (Sa Huynh), the Philippines (Tabon and Manunggul caves), Borneo, Sulawesi and the Sunda Arc [@Wu2021Prehistori; @Carro2024Prehistori]. In these jar cemeteries, defleshed human remains were placed inside large vessels alongside nephrite ear ornaments, carnelian beads and bronze bells.
- Elite metal-age burial wealth: By 500BC, mortuary inequality expanded markedly at sites like Ban Non Wat and Dong Son, where select graves contained hundreds of bronze axes, socketed lance points, ceremonial bells, cast bronze drums, biconical spindle whorls and gold leaf bangles [@Pryce2025Southeast].

## The Neolithic Transition and the Two-Layer Hypothesis

The emergence of sedentary food production in Southeast Asia is explained by the two-layer human dispersal model, supported by craniometrics and ancient genomics [@McColl2018Prehistori; @Matsumura2019Craniometr; @Matsumura2021Female]. Rather than an indigenous development, agricultural technologies were introduced through the southward migration of Neolithic farming populations from southern China beginning around 2500BC [@Wang2026Multiple; @Stoneking2023Genomic].

Ancient genomic sequences from northern Vietnam (Man Bac), central Thailand and southern China demonstrate that these migrant farmers carried ancestry derived from Yangtze and Yellow River agricultural populations [@McColl2018Prehistori; @Wang2026Multiple]. In Mainland Southeast Asia, Austroasiatic-speaking farming communities migrated along the river corridors of the Red River, Mekong and Chao Phraya [@Enfield2011Dynamics; @Matsumura2017Holocene]. They brought domestic rice, foxtail millet, domestic pigs, dogs and ceramic traditions characterised by incised, cord-marked and paddle-impressed pottery [@Matsumura2017Holocene; @Nelson2020Tracing].

Concurrently, Austronesian-speaking populations expanded southward from Taiwan into the northern Philippines (Luzon) around 2200BC, introducing red-slipped pottery, spindle whorls, bark-cloth beaters and polished stone adzes [@Wu2021Prehistori; @Nelson2020Tracing; @Stoneking2023Genomic]. From the Philippines, Austronesian maritime dispersals bifurcated: one branch moved southward into Sulawesi, the Moluccas and the Lesser Sunda Islands, while another moved southwestward into Borneo, Sumatra and Java [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Matsumura2018Cranio; @Suryatman2018Sakkarra].

At stratified sites such as Man Bac in the Red River Delta and Gua Harimau in Sumatra, human skeletal remains reveal cohabitation, intermarriage and biological admixture between incoming East Asian agriculturalists and indigenous Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers [@McColl2018Prehistori; @Matsumura2018Cranio; @Aghakhanian2022Sequence]. While agriculturalists occupied open floodplain terraces and coastal estuaries, indigenous foraging groups persisted in highland forests, engaging in reciprocal trade exchange of forest products for rice and polished stone tools [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Piper2017Perspectiv].

## The Metal Age Transformation and Regional Interaction Spheres

Between 1200BC and 500BC, Southeast Asia entered the Bronze and Iron Ages, triggering substantial demographic concentration and technological innovation [@Pryce2024Late; @Pryce2025Southeast]. Bivalve stone and ceramic moulds were deployed to cast socketed bronze adzes, lance points, fishhooks and bells. In the Khorat Plateau and central Thailand, extensive copper-mining and smelting complexes developed at Khao Wong Prachan and Sepon, providing metals for inter-regional exchange networks [@Pryce2025Southeast].

By 600BC, two prominent cultural spheres dominated mainland and coastal Southeast Asia:
1. The Dong Son culture in northern Vietnam: Situated in the Red River, Ma and Ca river valleys, Dong Son communities engineered intensive bunded wet-rice fields, constructed defended settlement earthworks and manufactured monumental bronze drums decorated with scenes of ceremonial warriors, longboats, birds and geometric motifs [@McColl2018Prehistori; @Pryce2025Southeast].
2. The Sa Huynh culture along the central and southern Vietnamese coast: Maritime-adapted communities developed extensive jar-burial necropolises, distinctive two-headed animal nephrite ear ornaments (*lingling-o*) and maritime trading networks linking coastal Vietnam with the Philippines, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula [@Wu2021Prehistori; @Carro2024Prehistori].

Simultaneously, iron metallurgy appeared around 500BC, providing durable tillage tools that facilitated forest clearance and hydraulic canal management in deep alluvial lowlands. In central Myanmar, Pyu walled settlements such as Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra began coalescing around agricultural and mineral extraction zones [@Pryce2024Late]. In insular Southeast Asia, glass beads and bronze kettle drums spread through maritime voyaging circuits, connecting island ports across Java, Bali and Sulawesi with mainland metallurgical centres [@Matsumura2018Cranio; @Suryatman2018Sakkarra].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To reconstruct demographic densities across 4.116.175 km² of terrestrial surface, the MANDALA spatial engine partitions prehistoric Southeast Asia into 52.603 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km). Each cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to perennial river stems (the Irrawaddy, Salween, Chao Phraya, Mekong, Red River, Kapuas, Barito and Musi), applying exponential density attenuation beyond 15 km in dense rainforest tracts [@Maxwell1999Holocene; @Pryce2025Southeast].
- Coastal proximity and estuarine weighting: favouring sheltered embayments, mangrove estuaries and coral reef zones suitable for maritime fishing, shell harvesting and waterborne transport [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Wu2021Prehistori].
- Volcanic soil fertility: elevating suitability scores across young Quaternary volcanic ash soils in Java, Bali and southern Sumatra, which sustain high agricultural carrying capacities compared to leached tropical oxisols [@Matsumura2018Cranio].
- Topographic slope: penalising steep mountainous terrain in the Annamite Range, Barisan Mountains, Shan Plateau and Central Cordillera of New Guinea and Luzon, while favouring flat alluvial plains and coastal bluffs [@Piper2017Perspectiv].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Density Modelling

To prevent double counting between nucleated settlement populations and dispersed rural inhabitants, 523 catalogued archaeological settlements with georeferenced WGS84 coordinates are linked to their chronological population trajectories. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary feathering algorithm smoothes density transitions across sub-regional frontiers, preventing step discontinuities along mountain divides and administrative limits.

## Carrying Capacity and Caloric Balancing

Demographic totals across each sub-region are cross-checked against ecological carrying capacities:
- Forager regimes: Baseline carrying capacities for equatorial rainforest foraging range from 0,05 to 0,35 persons per km² (5 to 35 persons per 100 km²), reflecting the dispersion of wild carbohydrates in climax dipterocarp canopies [@Piper2017Perspectiv; @Aghakhanian2022Sequence].
- Estuarine and coastal gathering: Coastal and mangrove ecozones supported substantially higher foraging densities (up to 1,5 to 3 persons per km²), sustained by dependable marine shellfish, tidal fish traps and mangrove crabs [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Matsumura2017Holocene].
- Early Neolithic horticulture: Mixed swidden vegeculture and dry-field millet-rice farming sustained densities between 2 and 8 persons per km² [@Wang2026Multiple; @Pryce2025Southeast].
- Intensive Metal-Age wet-rice systems: Bunded paddy agriculture in silted alluvial deltas and volcanic soils supported carrying capacities exceeding 25 to 70 persons per km² by 500BC, generating substantial caloric surpluses for non-farming craft specialists and political elites [@Pryce2025Southeast].

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and macro-regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 8% across all benchmark years from 10000BC to 500BC). At the 500BC apex, the regional total of 8,5M is bounded between 7,82M and 9,18M inhabitants. This uncertainty interval accommodates variances in archaeological site visibility, tropical vegetation overgrowth, radiocarbon calibration spans and differing house-mound multipliers [@Qiu2025Chronology; @Pryce2025Southeast].

# Testing and Validation

## Archaeogenetics and Ancient Genomic Corroboration

Recent advances in ancient DNA extraction have transformed Southeast Asian prehistoric demography [@McColl2018Prehistori; @Stoneking2023Genomic]. High-throughput sequencing of petrous bone samples from hunter-gatherer skeletons at Pha Faen in Laos and Gua Cha in Malaysia confirmed deep genomic affinities with Andamanese Onge and Australo-Papuan populations [@McColl2018Prehistori]. In contrast, skeletons from late third-millennium BC Neolithic contexts at Man Bac in northern Vietnam and Ban Chiang in Thailand demonstrate substantial East Asian ancestry related to Southern Han and Daic populations [@McColl2018Prehistori; @Wang2026Multiple].

Y-chromosome haplogroup sequencing confirms multiple southward expansions of patrilineal farming lineages (O1b1-M95 and O1a-M119) from southern China into Indochina and island Southeast Asia between 3000BC and 1000BC [@Wang2026Multiple]. Admixture analyses indicate that modern Malaysian indigenous groups retain 20% to 50% Hoabinhian ancestral components, demonstrating prolonged demographic interaction rather than total replacement [@Aghakhanian2022Sequence].

## Craniometrics and Skeletal Morphology

Cranio-morphometric analyses of over 500 prehistoric skulls from across eastern Eurasia corroborate the genomic findings [@Matsumura2008Terminal; @Matsumura2019Craniometr; @Matsumura2021Female]. Discriminant function and principal coordinate analyses demonstrate that terminal Pleistocene specimens from Hang Cho in Vietnam and Moh Khiew in Thailand cluster tightly with Australo-Melanesian populations, exhibiting low facial heights and prognathic profiles [@Matsumura2008Terminal; @Matsumura2021Female].

Beginning around 2000BC, female and male skeletal series across Indochina and the Indonesian archipelago show a decisive shift toward high facial profiles, flat nasal roots and globular crania characteristic of incoming East Asian populations [@Matsumura2018Cranio; @Matsumura2019Craniometr; @Matsumura2021Female]. At Gua Harimau in Sumatra, craniometric comparisons confirm that Neolithic individuals align with early Austronesian agriculturalists, confirming that population movements reached western Sundaland prior to the first millennium BC [@Matsumura2018Cranio].

## Palynological Records and Environmental Cores

Holocene sediment cores from across Southeast Asia document vegetation shifts that correspond with human demographic pulses [@Maxwell1999Holocene]. In Cambodia, pollen and micro-charcoal cores from the Tonle Sap basin and coastal estuaries reveal a prominent mid-Holocene expansion of disturbance taxa, including Poaceae and secondary pioneer shrubs, alongside elevated micro-charcoal concentrations [@Maxwell1999Holocene]. These environmental proxy signals indicate anthropogenic forest clearing for cultivation starting around 2500BC.

Similar palynological sequences from Lake Kumphawapi in northeastern Thailand and swamp cores from Sumatra and Borneo record significant declines in primary lowland dipterocarp rainforest [@Piper2017Perspectiv; @Pryce2025Southeast]. The corresponding increase in cultivated grasses and fire-tolerant vegetation validates the timing of agriculturalist settlement expansion reconstructed under MANDALA.

## Archaeometallurgical Sourcing and Lead Isotope Analyses

Copper and bronze artefacts across Southeast Asia have been systematically analysed using lead isotope ratios ($^{206}\text{Pb}/^{204}\text{Pb}$, $^{207}\text{Pb}/^{204}\text{Pb}$ and $^{208}\text{Pb}/^{204}\text{Pb}$) to reconstruct prehistoric exchange networks [@Pryce2024Late; @Pryce2025Southeast]. In the Khao Wong Prachan Valley of central Thailand, excavations at Non Pa Wai and Nil Kham Haeng uncovered extensive copper foundries producing thousands of ingot cakes and casting moulds [@Pryce2025Southeast].

Isotopic finger-printing demonstrates that copper smelted in Thailand and at the Sepon complex in central Laos was distributed over hundreds of kilometres, reaching late prehistoric settlements in the Red River Delta, Cambodia and peninsular Malaysia [@Pryce2024Late; @Pryce2025Southeast]. This metallurgical integration confirms that regional settlement hierarchies were linked by extensive riverine and coastal commodity circuits.

## Radiocarbon Chronologies and Bayesian Site Modelling

Regional settlement chronologies are anchored by extensive radiocarbon datasets [@Qiu2025Chronology; @Kaharudin2020Review]. In the Indonesian Archipelago, systematic review of cave and rockshelter dating projects highlights the importance of charcoal and short-lived seed samples over marine shell, which is prone to marine reservoir offsets [@Kaharudin2020Review].

Bayesian stratigraphic modelling at key multi-period sites has refined the timing of technological transitions:
- In central Myanmar, radiocarbon sequences from Halin establish four millennia of continuous habitation from late prehistoric foraging through the Pyu urban transition [@Pryce2024Late].
- In northern Vietnam and Thailand, AMS radiocarbon dates on rice phytoliths and carbonised grains confirm the presence of domestic rice agriculture by 2000BC [@Pryce2025Southeast].
- In the Philippines and Wallacea, short-lived botanical samples calibrate the initial arrival of red-slipped Austronesian pottery complexes to 2200BC in northern Luzon and 1800BC in Sulawesi and Timor [@Carro2022Talking; @Suryatman2018Sakkarra].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger was assembled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national archaeological registers and survey gazetteers, yielding 324 georeferenced settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of site catalogues from specialized excavation monographs and institutional reports, incorporating 141 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, adding 58 early Holocene rockshelters and open-air sites.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps across all eight divisions, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 832 candidate localities were audited: 523 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 309 were excluded (predominantly duplicate survey aliases within 2,2 km or modern administrative homonyms).

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### Terminal Pleistocene and Early Post-Glacial Foraging (10000BC to 6000BC)

During the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene, regional population expanded from 420k in 10000BC (yielding an aggregate density of 10,2 persons per 100 km²) to 580k in 8000BC and 950k in 6000BC (23,08 persons per 100 km²). As rising sea levels inundated the Sunda shelf, foraging groups concentrated along retreating coastlines, karst valleys and river confluences [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Kaharudin2020Review].

In northern Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia, Hoabinhian foragers exploited broad-spectrum rainforest resources, utilising smoke-dried preservation techniques and limestone rockshelters [@Matsumura2008Terminal; @Hung2025Earliest; @Stimpson2025Year].

In insular Wallacea, maritime foragers occupied caves on Timor, Alor and Sulawesi, exploiting offshore pelagic fish and marine molluscs [@Carro2022Talking; @Carro2024Prehistori].

### Mid-Holocene Environmental Stabilization and Early Horticultural Adaptations (6000BC to 3000BC)

Between 6000BC and 3000BC, global sea levels stabilised near modern shorelines, forming broad deltaic fan plains and estuarine mangrove complexes [@Maxwell1999Holocene]. Regional population rose from 950k in 6000BC to 1,75M in 4000BC and 2,85M by 3000BC (yielding an aggregate density of 69,24 persons per 100 km²).

Communities in coastal lowlands developed intensive shell-mound gathering economies (such as Da But in Vietnam and Khok Phanom Di in central Thailand), managing wild plants, taro tubers and arboricultural fruit trees [@Piper2017Perspectiv; @Matsumura2017Holocene].

In Borneo and Sumatra, foragers managed wild sago palm stands (*Metroxylon sagu*) and hunted bearded pigs, while early pottery traditions appeared across coastal nodes [@Curnoe2016Deep; @Piper2017Perspectiv].

### The Neolithic Expansion and Agriculturalist Dispersals (3000BC to 1200BC)

The arrival of agriculturalist populations from southern China triggered an unprecedented demographic surge [@McColl2018Prehistori; @Wang2026Multiple]. Between 3000BC and 1000BC, population expanded from 2,85M to 6,4M.

In mainland river valleys, Austroasiatic migrants cleared lowland forest to cultivate wet-rice and millets, establishing large open-air villages such as Phung Nguyen in the Red River Delta and Non Pa Wai in central Thailand [@Enfield2011Dynamics; @Pryce2025Southeast].

Concurrently, Austronesian-speaking maritime migrants expanded southward through the Philippines into Sulawesi, the Moluccas, Borneo and Java [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Matsumura2018Cranio; @Wu2021Prehistori]. They introduced red-slipped pottery, domesticated pigs, dogs and oceanic navigation techniques. By 2000BC, regional population reached 4,2M (102,04 persons per 100 km²), with agricultural farming villages flourishing along alluvial river levees and fertile volcanic terraces.

### The Metal Age Climax and Proto-Urban Nucleation (1200BC to 500BC)

The introduction of bronze metallurgy around 1200BC and iron working by 600BC initiated intensive craft specialisation, inter-regional exchange and settlement nucleation [@Pryce2024Late; @Pryce2025Southeast]. Regional population surged to 6,4M in 1000BC and culminated at 8,5M inhabitants at 500BC (yielding an aggregate density of 206,5 persons per 100 km²).

Major cultural complexes emerged across the landscape:
- In the Red River Delta, the Dong Son culture concentrated thousands of cultivators into fortified settlements, producing monumental bronze drums that served as insignia of administrative prestige and ritual authority [@Pryce2025Southeast].
- Along the central Vietnamese littoral, the Sa Huynh complex developed extensive maritime trading emporia, coordinating nephrite and glass bead trade with the Philippines and Borneo [@Wu2021Prehistori; @Carro2024Prehistori].
- In the Khorat Plateau of Thailand, settlements such as Ban Non Wat and Ban Chiang expanded into large earthen-mounded villages featuring stratified cemeteries with rich bronze grave goods [@Pryce2025Southeast].
- In central Myanmar, Pyu walled cities such as Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra began coalescing around irrigated agricultural tracts [@Pryce2024Late].
- In the Sunda Arc and Wallacea, maritime trading networks transported metal axes, bronze kettle drums and exotic spices between Java, Bali, Sulawesi and the Moluccas [@Matsumura2018Cranio; @Suryatman2018Sakkarra].

## Sub-Regional Chronological Trajectories

### Red River Delta, Annamite Cordillera and Lower Mekong

The northeastern mainland sector encompasses 500.116 km² of diverse deltaic silts, limestone karst formations and coastal embayments [@Matsumura2008Terminal; @McColl2018Prehistori]. From an initial population of 75,6k in 10000BC, demographic growth accelerated steadily through the Da But (ca. 5000BC) and Phung Nguyen (ca. 2000BC) horizons, reaching 756k in 2000BC, 1,15M in 1000BC and culminating at 1,53M in 500BC (305,93 persons per 100 km²).

Stratified excavation sequences at Dong Son, Man Bac, Hoa Lư and Đại La confirm that intensive wet-rice agriculture along the Red and Ma rivers sustained dense settlement agglomerations equipped with advanced bronze-casting facilities and monumental fortifications [@Pryce2025Southeast].

At Man Bac, craniometrics and ancient DNA prove co-existence and biological intermarriage between incoming East Asian agriculturalists and local Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers [@Matsumura2019Craniometr; @McColl2018Prehistori].

### Java, Bali and the Sunda Volcanic Arc

Encompassing 210.338 km² along the active subduction zone of southern Indonesia, the Sunda volcanic arc possessed exceptional soil fertility driven by Quaternary basaltic and andesitic tephra deposition [@Matsumura2018Cranio]. Population expanded from 71,4k in 10000BC to 297,5k in 4000BC, 714k in 2000BC and 1,45M in 500BC, attaining the highest sub-regional density across prehistoric Southeast Asia at 686,99 persons per 100 km².

Settlements such as Pain Haka in eastern Flores, together with early coastal trading stations across central Java and Bali, formed vital nodes in maritime exchange networks distributing bronze drums and marine products [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Matsumura2018Cranio].

Volcanic soils allowed continuous multi-cropping of root crops and wet-rice without the prolonged fallow periods required on mainland lateritic soils [@Matsumura2018Cranio].

### Chao Phraya, Khorat Plateau and Middle Mekong

Covering 757.362 km² across central and northeastern Thailand, Cambodia and Laos, this division supported major agricultural and metallurgical complexes [@Maxwell1999Holocene; @Pryce2025Southeast]. Population increased from 58,8k in 10000BC to 245k in 4000BC, 588k in 2000BC and 1,19M in 500BC (157,12 persons per 100 km²).

Key sites including Ban Non Wat, Ban Chiang, Non Nok Tha and the Plain of Jars reveal transitions from foraging and early millet-rice horticulture to intensive bronze casting supported by industrial copper smelting at Khao Wong Prachan and Sepon [@Pryce2025Southeast].

Surveys in the Mun and Chi river valleys demonstrate a dramatic increase in mounded settlement counts and artificial water storage ponds after 1000BC [@Pryce2025Southeast].

### Irrawaddy-Salween Basins and Arakan Uplands

Occupying 700.767 km² across western Myanmar and adjacent uplands, this corridor provided a natural terrestrial bridge connecting South Asia with mainland Indochina [@Pryce2024Late]. Regional population expanded from 54,6k in 10000BC to 227,5k in 4000BC, 546k in 2000BC and 1,11M in 500BC (157,68 persons per 100 km²).

Stratified sequences from Halin, Beikthano, Sri Ksetra and Nyaunggan demonstrate continuous occupation from late prehistoric lithic traditions through copper-bronze casting to proto-urban Pyu settlements [@Pryce2024Late].

Excavations in the Samon Valley reveal affluent Iron Age cemeteries where individuals were interred with bronze armlets, carnelian beads and cast copper mirrors [@Pryce2024Late].

### Malay Peninsula and Sumatra (Sundaland West)

Comprising 613.435 km² across the maritime strait linking the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, this division transitioned from continuous Sundaland lowland rainforest to a drowned littoral corridor [@Aghakhanian2022Sequence; @Matsumura2018Cranio]. Population grew from 54,6k in 10000BC to 227,5k in 4000BC, 546k in 2000BC and 1,11M in 500BC (180,13 persons per 100 km²).

Hoabinhian rockshelters such as Gua Cha and Gua Harimau reveal gradual cultural blending between indigenous forest foragers and incoming Austronesian maritime agriculturalists [@Matsumura2018Cranio; @Aghakhanian2022Sequence].

Coastal shell middens in the Malacca Strait document intensive exploitation of marine estuaries alongside early coastal ceramic production [@Bulbeck2008Integrated].

### Philippine Archipelago

Extending across 300.894 km² from Batanes and Luzon south to Mindanao, the Philippine archipelago acted as the primary gateway for the Austronesian diaspora into island Southeast Asia [@Wu2021Prehistori; @Stoneking2023Genomic]. Population grew from 46,2k in 10000BC to 192,5k in 4000BC, 462k in 2000BC and 935k in 500BC (310,74 persons per 100 km²).

Stratified settlement sequences at Nagsabaran in the Cagayan Valley, together with rockshelters in Palawan and western Luzon, document the arrival of red-slipped pottery, spindle whorls, nephrite ornaments and domestic pigs around 2200BC [@Nelson2020Tracing; @Wu2021Prehistori].

Lal-lo shell middens along the lower Cagayan River reflect dense riverine fishing communities managing freshwater bivalves (*Batissa childreni*) and rice agriculture [@Piper2017Perspectiv].

### Sulawesi, Maluku and the Wallacea-Timor Arc

Occupying 286.499 km² east of Wallace's Line, this oceanic island realm supported specialised maritime foraging communities that adopted Austronesian farming and metalworking [@Carro2022Talking; @Suryatman2018Sakkarra]. Population climbed from 33,6k in 10000BC to 140k in 4000BC, 336k in 2000BC and 680k in 500BC (237,35 persons per 100 km²).

Stratified sites such as Minanga Sipakko along the Karama River of western Sulawesi and Tron Bon Lei on Alor Island document transitions from pelagic maritime foraging to sedentary ceramic and metalworking villages [@Carro2022Talking; @Suryatman2018Sakkarra].

Deep oceanic passages fostered seafaring exchange in obsidian, chert and prestige shell items [@Carro2024Prehistori].

### Borneo River Basins (Niah and Mahakam)

Spanning 746.764 km² of dense equatorial rainforest and extensive river networks, Borneo accommodated 25,2k people in 10000BC, 105k in 4000BC, 252k in 2000BC and 510k in 500BC (68,29 persons per 100 km²).

Due to heavily leached tropical soils, agricultural populations developed swidden cultivation, riverine hunting and sago extraction [@Curnoe2016Deep; @Piper2017Perspectiv].

Sites such as Niah Cave in Sarawak and Bukit Tengkorak in Sabah acted as long-lived habitation centres and industrial workshops for obsidian blade manufacture and pottery production [@Curnoe2016Deep; @Piper2017Perspectiv].

The prehistoric settlement hierarchy comprised four functional tiers:
1. Primary nucleated centres (> 3k inhabitants): Dong Son Type-Site (5,66k in 500BC) and Sa Huynh (4,72k in 500BC) in Vietnam; Beikthano (3,5k in 500BC), Sri Ksetra (3,5k in 500BC) and Halin (3,5k in 500BC) in Myanmar; Hoa Lư (3,5k in 500BC) and Đại La (3,5k in 500BC) in northern Vietnam. These centres coordinated regional craft production, agricultural hydraulic engineering and long-distance maritime exchange.
2. Major regional centres (1,5k to 3k inhabitants): Ban Non Wat (2,38k peak, 1,88k in 500BC), Plain of Jars (2,3k peak, 2,04k in 500BC), Ban Chiang (1,94k peak), Khao Wong Prachan (1,8k peak) and the Samon Valley bronze sites (1,73k peak). These sites commanded major mineral deposits, copper smelting foundries and upland agricultural valleys.
3. Secondary agricultural towns and ports (800 to 1,5k inhabitants): Mimotien circular earthworks (1,53k peak), Phung Nguyen (1,38k peak), Sepon Copper Complex (1,36k peak), Nagsabaran (1,24k peak in the Philippines), Non Nok Tha (1,16k peak), Minanga Sipakko (1,08k peak in Sulawesi), Nyaunggan (1,02k peak) and Pain Haka (800 peak in the Sunda Arc).
4. Tertiary hamlets, rockshelters and coastal gathering camps (< 800 inhabitants): Bukit Tengkorak (698 peak), Khok Phanom Di (660 peak), Man Bac (660 peak), Gua Cha, Hang Cho, Niah Cave and hundreds of rural agrarian hamlets catalogued throughout the region.

# Limitations

Archaeological visibility and demographic reconstruction in prehistoric Southeast Asia are subject to severe taphonomic constraints:
1. Tropical soil acidity and organic degradation: humid monsoonal climates and acidic lateritic soils cause rapid dissolution of unburned organic materials, destroying wood architecture, woven textiles, bone implements and plant remains outside waterlogged or dry cave environments [@Piper2017Perspectiv; @Nelson2020Tracing].
2. Fluvial sedimentation and coastal drowning: dynamic river systems (such as the Red River, Mekong and Chao Phraya) deposit metres of silt annually, burying early Holocene settlements beneath deep alluvial overburden [@Maxwell1999Holocene; @Pryce2025Southeast]. Furthermore, post-glacial sea level rise submerged vast expanses of Sundaland, placing terminal Pleistocene coastal settlements under tens of metres of seawater [@Bulbeck2008Integrated; @Kaharudin2020Review].
3. Modern agricultural transformation and urbanization: deep mechanised rice cultivation, shrimp farming in coastal estuaries and urban construction in metropolitan centres such as Hanoi, Bangkok and Jakarta have disturbed ancient archaeological mounds and shell middens [@Pryce2025Southeast].
4. Anisotropic survey intensity: archaeological fieldwork has concentrated heavily in accessible river valleys of Thailand and northern Vietnam, while interior rainforest basins in Borneo, Sumatra and Sulawesi have received lower systematic survey coverage [@Kaharudin2020Review; @Suryatman2018Sakkarra].

# Conclusion

Prehistoric Southeast Asia experienced profound demographic expansion from 420k terminal Pleistocene foragers in 10000BC to an all-time prehistoric apex of 8,5M inhabitants at 500BC across 4,12M km² of territory. This growth was underpinned by three transformative developments: the adaptation of broad-spectrum Hoabinhian foragers to retreating post-glacial shorelines, the southward dispersal of Austroasiatic and Austronesian agriculturalists introducing wet-rice farming, domestic animals and pottery, and the emergence of specialised bronze and iron metallurgical networks linking mainland river valleys with insular maritime ports.

Demographic mass concentrated most heavily in the silt-renewed floodplains of the Red River Delta and the volcanic terranes of Java and Bali, where intensive agricultural systems generated large food surpluses capable of sustaining dense nucleated communities. By integrating georeferenced settlement trajectories with ancient genomic evidence, craniometric datasets, sediment pollen records and radiocarbon calibrations, this study establishes a quantitative baseline for the study of Southeast Asian prehistory prior to the rise of classical Indianised and Sinicised kingdoms in the first millennium AD.
